uncited: This family encompasses methods that accelerate the conversion of geometric sources (meshes, point clouds) into discrete volumetric representations by leveraging parallel processing units, primarily GPUs via CUDA or OpenGL/Vulkan, and multi-threaded CPUs.
It solves the performance bottleneck of naive, single-threaded voxelization algorithms, enabling real-time or near-real-time processing for complex models.

It differs from its siblings by explicitly utilizing hardware parallelism (thread-per-triangle, thread-per-voxel, or rasterization pipelines) and specialized memory structures (atomic counters, bit-packed tables, MSAA coverage) to handle the massive concurrency inherent in volumetric data generation.
Perform normal-based classification and bucket sorting for polygonal models.
Encode and store results as 2D textures in three directional sheet buffers.
- **Definition**: A technique to fix 'cracks' (holes/slots) in voxelization caused by steep primitive slopes relative to the view direction.
- Swizzle the X, Y, and Z components of the vertex positions in the Geometry Shader to change the projection direction.
- **Formula**: Crack Condition: If $|ddx(depth)| > 1.0$ or $|ddy(depth)| > 1.0$, cracks occur perpendicular to the depth direction.
The acceleration of voxelization has been driven by the need for real-time simulation and rendering of complex phenomena, such as fluids and deformable objects.
Early approaches relied on CPU-based parallelization or simple rasterization techniques.
The introduction of GPU-based methods, particularly those utilizing CUDA and advanced OpenGL/Vulkan features like MSAA and atomic operations, allowed for significant performance gains.

It selects the projection direction (X, Y, or Z axis) based on the face normal to present the largest face area, avoiding high depth gradients [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the technique selects the projection direction (X, Y, or Z axis) based on the face normal to present the largest face area, thereby avoiding high depth gradients. The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly confirms this: 'To fix this issue, primitives need to be rendered from an axis that presents the largest face area with respect to the camera. In other words, from a camera direction selected from the X, Y and Z axes according to the face normal.' It further states that this method allows one to 'avoid the issue of missing voxels caused by high depth gradients.' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
